summary: Defines what network renumbering is and discusses why an organization might need to change its addresses. It is informational and sets up the background for the renumbering guide that follows.

eli5.summary: If you move to a new street, every sign pointing to your house needs updating. This note explains why and when networks must do the same.

subtitle: What it means to renumber a network and the many reasons an organization may have to do it.

tldr.problem: More organizations were connecting to the Internet, often with addresses that were non-unique, oversized, or borrowed from a provider, and the idea of network renumbering needed a clear definition.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines renumbering as changing the IP host addresses, and perhaps the network mask, of devices in a network, then sorts the reasons for doing it into past, present and future groups.
tldr.outcome: It is background for the PIER working group's renumbering documents and does not describe methods or tools. Its advice is to allocate addresses with care and be prepared to renumber.

today: RFC 2071 is an Informational RFC, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is companion background to RFC 2072, the Router Renumbering Guide.

sections.title: Why Addresses Are Borrowed
sections.content:
Reaching any destination on the global Internet relies on unique IP host addresses. A duplicate address would make one of the destinations unreachable from some origins, although globally unique addresses are not always necessary, depending on connectivity needs.

Address registries such as the InterNIC, and ISPs, had become more prudent. Under the InterNIC policy, most end-user networks get their addresses from their upstream ISP, except where dual-homing, multihoming or very large blocks are needed. So end users cannot assume they own their addresses; they borrow part of a provider's allocation, which was assigned in a way consistent with global routing.

Not having permanent addresses does not remove stable identifiers: DNS names identify servers and workstations, and DHCP can help automate assigning names and the borrowed addresses.
sections.eli5: Most families rent their address from the neighborhood landlord instead of owning it, so if they switch landlords the address has to change. Names stay the same, like a nickname.

sections.title: What Renumbering Means
sections.content:
In the simplest definition, renumbering is changing the IP host addresses, and perhaps the network mask, of every device in the network that has an address. It may cover only some networks in a domain, or all the networks of an autonomous system.

Affected devices include PCs, workstations, printers, file servers, terminal servers and routers. Renumbering can also mean editing configuration files that hold addresses, such as those listing DNS servers, SNMP management stations and access control lists.

It need not be sudden. Upstream providers will often allow a grace period when the old and new addresses are both usable in parallel. The memo does not cover renumbering methods, techniques or tools.
sections.eli5: Renumbering is giving every device in the building a new house number and then fixing every list that still has the old one.

sections.title: Reasons from the Past
sections.content:
Many networks were built with IP for ordinary data communication, using unregistered, non-unique addresses. Once Internet connectivity became valuable they could no longer use them. Network Address Translation (NAT) and private address space can cut the number of unique addresses needed and localize the changes, though NAT may not be viable at some scales or topologies.

Some organizations received very large "Class A" or "Class B" allocations and could manage with a smaller CIDR block, and might be asked to return the old allocation. Others must move from bridged networks to routed ones, which requires subnetting. Older routing protocols such as RIP and IGRP advertise many updates, while OSPF, EIGRP and IS-IS work best with structured addressing that allows aggregation.

Poorly structured address space also makes it hard to delegate address administration. The memo observes that a good numbering plan is also a good renumbering plan, and that renumbering without a host inventory (absent DHCP) is not possible.
sections.eli5: Some towns grew without a street plan, then needed one. Fixing it means changing a lot of house numbers.

sections.title: Reasons in the Present
sections.content:
Mergers, acquisitions and reorganizations can force networks with different prefixes to be blended. Two enterprises linked by private circuits may both use private address space and risk duplicate addresses, so one or both may need to renumber or obtain unique registered addresses.

Changing ISP is the best-known case. Because the old ISP announces its CIDR block as a single prefix, a former customer advertising a piece of it would add a routing entry to the global table, which the memo calls "punching holes" in a CIDR block. If done at scale the table could grow too large for backbone routers, so ISPs discourage it and some write it into contracts. The memo says the likelihood of being forced to renumber is inversely related to the size of the customer's space (a /16 may be treated as portable; several scattered /24s may not), and that this renumbering is a technical consequence, not a commercial or political mandate.

Other drivers are registry rules requiring justified usage, workgroup LAN switches and VLANs (moving a host between VLANs moves it to another subnet), and NBMA services such as frame relay, where treating each virtual circuit as a /30 subnet calls for variable length subnet masks. Dialup growth, and returning scattered prefixes for one aggregate that suits classless routing, are also named.
sections.eli5: Switching providers is like switching phone companies: the number belongs to the company, and a big, tidy block of numbers is easier for everyone to keep track of.

sections.title: Future Reasons and Summary
sections.content:
Looking ahead, switched virtual circuit services such as ATM may use cut-through paths and an address resolution server (Next Hop Resolution Protocol), whose database and client settings would be affected by renumbering. A move to IPv6 would also require renumbering, perhaps not immediately, and at least DNS entries and router-advertised prefixes would change.

The summary cites the IAB's view that renumbering is becoming more widespread and commonplace. Because even the best foresight cannot rule it out, the advice is to allocate carefully at the start and to be prepared. The security note adds that renumbering can defeat security systems based on static IP addresses, so they need special care.
sections.eli5: New kinds of roads and maps keep arriving, so one day you may need to change your address again. The best plan is to keep a tidy list and expect it.
